01 / The overlap

The laboratory is where I learned what a system has to survive.

A result has to be traceable. A checklist has to be followed. A stock record has to match what is on the shelf. Those habits follow me into software.

I am a Registered Laboratory Technician with a Diploma in Biomedical Sciences with Distinction. I also carry the ICT work at district level when machines fail or a paper process needs a better system.

The two roles are not separate identities to me. In diagnostics, small gaps become serious errors. In software, the same is true. My work starts with the real workflow: who records what, where information gets lost, what still has to function without internet, and what a person needs to see before making a decision.

CASE NOTE 001
HEALTH OPERATIONS
OFFLINE-FIRST

iCMS

Integrated Clinic Management System
  • Context
    Clinic operations
  • Problem
    Disconnected records
  • Constraint
    Unreliable connectivity
  • Status
    Leased to private clinics

The problem I was looking at

Laboratory, pharmacy and administration can operate as separate islands. When their records do not meet, stock movement, payments and service activity are harder to reconcile. Those gaps can create room for drug loss, financial leakage and missed revenue.

The decision that shaped it

I made iCMS offline-first. A district-health tool cannot assume continuous internet or stable power, then call the resulting downtime an edge case. The core workflow has to remain useful under the conditions where it will actually be used.

What I built into the working system

iCMS brings operational records into one system instead of treating each department as an isolated process. These are the confirmed modules I have built:

  • MODULE 01Stock and inventory
  • MODULE 02Automated laboratory roster
  • MODULE 03Digitized laboratory checklists

A look through the working system

These screens are from iCMS as I built it. The patient names, counts and transactions shown here are demo/test data, not live clinic records.

02 / How I work

I start with the point where the real work gets stuck.

No screen begins as “a feature.” It begins as a handoff, record, delay or repeated piece of work that needs to be understood first.

Follow the workflow

I write down who does the work, what they record, and where the next person depends on that record. That exposes the gaps before code hides them.

Name the constraint

At district-hospital level, power and connectivity are operating conditions—not footnotes. I decide what must still work when either one disappears.

Build the useful core

I keep the first version close to the task: stock, a roster, a checklist. The interface should make the process clearer, not merely move the paperwork onto a screen.

Leave an audit trail

My laboratory background keeps me focused on records that can be followed and checked. If a system cannot help someone understand what happened, it is not finished.

Design correction / what the first assumption gets wrong

“Online all the time” is not a safe starting point.

A polished cloud workflow is still the wrong tool if it stops the moment the network does. My correction was structural, not cosmetic: make offline use part of the core design. That tradeoff means choosing reliability and continuity over features that only look impressive in a perfect demo environment.
